name: Simvastatin
summary: Simvastatin is a statin, a medicine that lowers cholesterol by reducing how much the liver makes, and it is used to treat high cholesterol and to help prevent heart disease, including heart attacks and strokes. Serious side effects are uncommon, but the NHS advises seeking help from a doctor for unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness, and a GP or NHS 111 is the route for prompt advice. Grapefruit juice, some antibiotics such as clarithromycin and several other medicines can raise simvastatin levels and the risk of muscle damage.
usedFor: Lowering cholesterol in people who have been diagnosed with high blood cholesterol
Helping to prevent heart disease, including heart attacks and strokes
A doctor may prescribe it when there is a family history of heart disease or a long-term condition such as rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes or type 2 diabetes
howItWorks: Simvastatin stops the liver from making cholesterol, which lowers the level of cholesterol in the blood. It belongs to the group of medicines called statins, also known as HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors.
onset: The NHS says treatment is usually long term, and it takes some weeks for cholesterol levels to fall.

common: Headache, dizziness and feeling sick are listed by the NHS as common side effects.
Digestive problems and sleep problems are also listed as common.
Muscle aches are also listed as common, and the NHS says unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness should be reported to a doctor.
serious: Unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps can be a sign of muscle breakdown that may damage the kidneys; the NHS says this can appear weeks or months after starting, and a GP or NHS 111 is the route for prompt advice.

Yellowing of the skin or eyes, or pale stools with dark urine, can point to liver problems; the NHS notes yellowing is harder to see on brown or black skin, and a GP or NHS 111 should be contacted promptly.
Severe stomach pain, which can be a sign of pancreatitis, or a pink-red rash needs prompt advice from a GP or NHS 111.
A serious allergic reaction, with breathing or swallowing problems or a swollen face or throat, is an emergency, and the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E.

cautions: Grapefruit juice raises the level of simvastatin in the blood and makes side effects more likely, and the NHS says to avoid it.
NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance lists clarithromycin as contraindicated with simvastatin and says that, if the antibiotic is essential, simvastatin is stopped for the course.

The NHS lists other medicines that raise the risk of muscle damage, including the antibiotics clarithromycin, rifampicin and fusidic acid, the antifungals fluconazole and ketoconazole, some HIV medicines, hepatitis C treatments, warfarin, ciclosporin and danazol.
If one of those medicines is needed, the doctor may lower the simvastatin dose, switch to a different statin or pause simvastatin for a while.
The product information (SmPC) limits the simvastatin dose with some heart medicines, such as amlodipine, so the prescriber takes this into account.
The NHS says drinking a lot of alcohol may increase the chance of muscle and liver side effects.

The NHS lists liver or kidney problems, lung disease, an underactive thyroid, a past muscle disorder, a history of myasthenia gravis and regularly drinking large amounts of alcohol as reasons to check with a doctor before taking simvastatin.
The NHS says simvastatin is not recommended in pregnancy because it can affect how the baby develops, and it gives separate advice for people planning a pregnancy.
It is not usually used in breastfeeding because it is not known whether it passes into breast milk, and a doctor may suggest a different statin.
The NHS says there is not enough information about herbal remedies and supplements taken with simvastatin, because they are generally not tested for their effect on other medicines.
The NHS advises against stopping simvastatin without medical advice, because cholesterol may rise and the risk of heart attacks and strokes may go up.
monitoring: The NHS says that during the first 12 months of treatment a couple of routine tests are offered to check that the liver is working properly.
regimenNote: Tablets and an oral liquid (suspension) that are swallowed; also available in combination tablets with other cholesterol-lowering medicines.

sections.heading: What is simvastatin used for?
sections.body:
Simvastatin is a type of medicine called a statin. The NHS says it is used to lower cholesterol in people who have been diagnosed with high blood cholesterol. It is also used to help prevent heart disease, including heart attacks and strokes. A doctor may prescribe it when there is a family history of heart disease or a long-term condition such as rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes or type 2 diabetes.

Most adults can take simvastatin, and the NHS says it is sometimes prescribed to children aged 10 and over. It comes as tablets and as a liquid that is swallowed, and it is also available in combination tablets with other cholesterol-lowering medicines. In the UK, many simvastatin products are sold under the generic name, and the brand name Zocor also appears in the electronic Medicines Compendium. The NHS describes treatment as usually long term.

sections.heading: How does simvastatin work?
sections.body:
Simvastatin stops the liver from making cholesterol, which lowers the level of cholesterol in the blood. It belongs to the group of medicines also known as HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors. Lowering cholesterol is one way of reducing the risk of heart attacks and strokes in people at high risk.

The NHS says it takes some weeks for cholesterol levels to fall. Because simvastatin works on cholesterol levels rather than on symptoms, a person may feel no different while taking it.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of simvastatin?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headache, dizziness, feeling sick, digestive problems, muscle aches and sleep problems as common side effects. It says serious side effects are uncommon, affecting fewer than 1 in 1,000 people.

Muscle problems are the ones to watch for. The NHS advises seeking help from a doctor for unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps, which can signal muscle breakdown and kidney damage and can appear weeks or months after starting. A GP or NHS 111 is the route for prompt advice.

Yellowing of the skin or eyes, or pale stools with dark urine, can point to liver problems, and the NHS notes yellowing is harder to see on brown or black skin. Severe stomach pain, which can be a sign of pancreatitis, and a pink-red rash are also listed as serious effects. For breathing or swallowing problems, or a swollen face or throat, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E.

sections.heading: Taking simvastatin with other medicines, grapefruit or alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says grapefruit juice increases the level of simvastatin in the blood and makes side effects more likely, so it advises avoiding it. Some medicines also raise the risk of serious side effects such as muscle damage. The NHS lists the antibiotics clarithromycin, rifampicin and fusidic acid, the antifungals fluconazole and ketoconazole, some HIV medicines, hepatitis C treatments, warfarin, ciclosporin and danazol.

NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance lists clarithromycin as contraindicated with simvastatin. Where such a medicine is needed, the doctor may lower the simvastatin dose, switch to a different statin or pause simvastatin for a while. The product information also limits the simvastatin dose with some heart medicines, such as amlodipine.

The NHS says drinking a lot of alcohol may increase the chance of muscle and liver side effects. It says there is not enough information about herbal remedies and supplements taken with simvastatin. A pharmacist or doctor can check any new medicine against simvastatin.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and what about pregnancy?
sections.body:
The NHS says simvastatin may not be suitable for people with liver or kidney problems, lung disease or an underactive thyroid. A past muscle disorder, a history of myasthenia gravis and regularly drinking large amounts of alcohol are other reasons to check with a doctor first. People are also asked to tell the doctor about unexplained ongoing muscle pain or a family history of muscle problems.

The NHS says simvastatin is not recommended in pregnancy because it can affect how the baby develops, and it gives separate advice for people planning a pregnancy. It is not usually used in breastfeeding because it is not known whether it passes into breast milk, and a doctor may suggest a different statin. During the first 12 months of treatment, a couple of routine tests are offered to check that the liver is working properly. The NHS advises against stopping simvastatin without medical advice, because cholesterol may rise and the risk of heart attacks and strokes may go up.

faqs.q: Can I drink grapefruit juice while taking simvastatin?
faqs.a: The NHS says grapefruit juice increases the level of simvastatin in the blood, which makes side effects more likely. It therefore advises avoiding grapefruit juice with simvastatin. A pharmacist or doctor can say how this applies to an individual.

faqs.q: Can I take clarithromycin with simvastatin?
faqs.a: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance lists clarithromycin as contraindicated with simvastatin. If the antibiotic is essential, the guidance is that simvastatin is stopped for the course. The prescriber decides what happens in each case, so the doctor or pharmacist should be told about any antibiotic.

faqs.q: What should I do about muscle pain on simvastatin?
faqs.a: The NHS advises seeking help from a doctor for unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps. These can be a sign of muscle breakdown and kidney damage, and can appear weeks or months after starting. A GP appointment or NHS 111 is the route, and the NHS advises against stopping simvastatin without medical advice.

faqs.q: Can simvastatin be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says simvastatin is not recommended in pregnancy because it can affect how the baby develops. It gives separate advice for people planning a pregnancy. It is not usually used in breastfeeding either, and a doctor may suggest a different statin.

faqs.q: Are blood tests needed with simvastatin?
faqs.a: The NHS says that during the first 12 months of treatment a couple of routine tests are offered to check that the liver is working properly. Yellowing of the skin or eyes, or pale stools with dark urine, can point to liver problems and should be reported to a GP or NHS 111 promptly.
